name: type-object
intent: Lift part of the type system out of the class hierarchy and into data: one descriptor object holds everything shared by all instances of a conceptual type, every instance holds a reference to its type object and delegates type-specific requests to it, and new types are therefore created and tuned as data instead of as compiled code.
problem: Each new kind of thing forces a new subclass, and each tweak to a kind's shared values forces an edit and a rebuild, because the differences between the kinds are expressed in the type system rather than in data - while the people who own those differences (designers, domain experts, tenants) cannot ship a build.
context: Applies where an object model has a large, open, frequently tuned set of conceptually identical kinds whose differences are mostly data (stats, labels, thresholds, formats, layouts) with only a small fixed repertoire of behaviour; where instances outnumber type definitions by orders of magnitude and all instances of one kind must share their type-level data; and where the deployment loop is expensive (shipped binaries, on-premise installs, store review) but the data can be edited at runtime. It is the object-level, in-memory cousin of metadata-driven architectures such as adaptive object models.
benefits: New types are created and tuned without recompiling: type definitions can be authored in files, databases or admin screens and become effective on the next load.
Subclass explosion is avoided: one instance class plus N type objects replaces N subclasses whose only job was to carry different constants.
Instance-handling code stays uniform and small: one class, one construction path, no per-type overrides to keep in sync.
Type data is shared: every instance of a type references the same descriptor instead of duplicating its constants, which saves memory and keeps the values consistent.
An instance can change its type at runtime by pointing at another type object, which is far simpler than migrating an object to another class.
Type definitions become data that can be validated, versioned, migrated and diffed like any other configuration.
tradeoffs: Design complexity: one logical object is factored into two things, and the relationship between a thing and its type is genuinely harder to explain and to keep straight - the originating paper's own summary of the force is 'use inheritance; it's easier'.

Implementation complexity: behaviour that used to be an overridden method becomes state in the descriptor, so genuinely different algorithms no longer have a natural code home and must be squeezed into data or function slots.

Reference management becomes the application's job: unlike a class link, the instance-to-type-object reference is established, kept valid and torn down by hand, and nothing in the compiler enforces it.
Type bookkeeping: descriptors must be loaded, registered and kept alive at least as long as any instance referring to them - lifecycle work the compiler used to do automatically.

Type errors move to runtime: a mistyped id, an unvalidated data file or a missing registration yields a broken instance instead of a compile error; the system now has to provide its own type checking.
Tooling blindness: types are no longer in the type system, so IDEs, refactoring tools and static analysis cannot see or check them.
An extra indirection (usually a lookup as well) sits on every type-specific access: negligible for long-lived objects, visible in hot loops over flat data.
Once adopted, type objects attract composition and authoring tools until the descriptor structure itself becomes complex - the paper warns that this 'hard part' arrives only after first use.

participants.responsibility: Holds everything shared by all instances of one conceptual type - data (stats, labels, thresholds, formats) and the behaviour slots the type needs; one instance of the type class represents one logical type and is shared by every instance of that type.

Carries the state that differs per instance (current health, position, level, dirty flags), holds a reference to its type object and delegates type-specific requests to it; it is an instance of exactly one typed class.

The class of type objects: defines what a type definition is in this model, owns the creation of type objects (including the factory method that instantiates typed objects, so construction has one path) and may carry the reverse link to the objects of that type.

The class of typed objects: defines the messages an instance understands and decides for each of them whether it is answered locally or forwarded to the type object - a type object cannot add messages the typed class does not declare.

The lookup (type table / type store) that maps a stable id to the type object currently registered for it and is populated from external data at load time; it is the single source of truth for which types exist.

Works with typed objects through the typed class's interface and is normally unaware of the split; code that creates or looks up types (loaders, editors, spawners) may collaborate with the type objects directly.

use_cases: Game and simulation content: monster breeds, item, spell and vehicle definitions whose stat blocks are authored by designers in JSON or a database while the code only knows how to use a descriptor.

Adaptive object models and metadata-driven business systems: entity types and attribute types defined at runtime (the Type Square combination of Type Object with the Property pattern), so users add new business entity kinds without a deployment.
Product and tariff catalogs: insurance products, telecom plans, loan products or workflow step types whose differences are field values plus a behaviour chosen from a fixed repertoire.
Rule, report and form definitions: document templates, report layouts, validation rule sets and form definitions loaded from configuration, where each definition is a type of document.
Plugin and format registries: file-format definitions, protocol dialects, connector kinds and decoder tables that must be extended after the binary or container has shipped.
Test and demo data: defining many fixture 'kinds' as data so a data-driven path can be exercised over dozens of variants without writing dozens of classes.

Unity's ScriptableObject assets: a gameplay class (e.g. a spawner or vehicle controller) holds a reference to a ScriptableObject asset that centralizes shared type parameters - the Unity docs' own example is a VehicleTypeInfo asset with one asset file per vehicle kind - so designers tweak or add type assets in the editor while the code keeps a single consuming class.

Salesforce custom objects: admins author an object as data (a CustomObject definition with a fields array via the Metadata API) and every record is handled by the platform's generic sObject CRUD and describe machinery - Type Object and the adaptive object model running in production at multi-tenant scale, with the Metadata API as the type registry.

Minecraft item and entity definitions: the engine ships one item implementation per behaviour and loads each item's identity, components and defaults from JSON item definitions in datapacks/behavior packs at world load, so modders and map makers add new item 'kinds' as pure data files without touching the binary.
avoid_when: The set of types is small, closed and known at compile time: an enum, sealed hierarchy or algebraic data type compiles the checks and gives exhaustiveness instead of moving them into data.

Type-specific behaviour dominates and each type implements genuinely different algorithms: subclasses, trait objects or strategy objects express that directly, while a descriptor with function slots mostly re-implements a vtable.
The type data never changes between builds and no non-programmer edits it: compile it in and let the language check it.

A configuration or plugin layer already provides validated, versioned, typed extensibility (schema-driven config, a plugin registry with typed factories) - type objects would duplicate that layer without adding reach.

Hot flat-data processing where one indirection per element costs more than type flexibility is worth: data-oriented layouts (archetype tables, column stores) are the alternative, not a descriptor reference per record.
anti_patterns: Using type objects for a set of kinds that is actually closed, and thereby trading compile-time type errors and exhaustive switches for unvalidated runtime data.
Mutating a registered type object in place: every existing instance silently changes with it, and instances created before and after the edit disagree about the type's values.
Storing per-instance state (current health, position, dirty flags) in the type object, so all instances of the type share it.
Addressing types by bare string literals at every call site instead of through a registry lookup with a fail-fast unknown-id error, so typos become silent misbehaviour.
Building the descriptor-composition system and the authoring tooling before a single type has been authored as data - the paper's 'hard part occurs after it has been used'.
Encapsulating the type object completely while making it the only way to construct instances, so no client can ever spawn an instance of a type it holds.
design_principles: Separate what varies per instance from what is shared per type.
Push the parts of the type system that must change at runtime out of code and into data.
Prefer composition over inheritance: an object has a type instead of being a subclass.
One authoritative descriptor per type, shared by all of its instances.
Keep published type data immutable so type identity stays stable.
best_practices: Load type definitions from external data at startup, validate them (ids, required fields, ranges, cross-references) and register them under stable ids; treat the registry as the single source of truth.
Keep registered descriptors immutable and derive tuned variants as new descriptors instead of editing a shared one.
Keep only type-level data and behaviour on the descriptor; all per-instance state stays on the instance.
Put a factory method on the type object (new_instance()) so allocation and initialisation have exactly one path per type.
Resolve type ids once (enum, handle or cached pointer) and avoid repeated string lookups in hot paths.
Guarantee descriptor lifetime: the registry outlives every instance, or instances share ownership of their descriptor.
Fail fast on unknown type ids and invalid type data - the system now owns the type checking the compiler used to do.
Version and migrate type data, and review type definitions like code, because they change behaviour without a build.
sources: Johnson, R. and Woolf, B., 'Type Object', in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (PLoPD3), Addison-Wesley, 1998, ch. 4.
